nameStory: The Umbrella Jelly gets its name from its distinctive bell-shaped body that looks remarkably like a tiny, translucent umbrella floating through the water. When you see one pulsing along, it's easy to imagine it as nature's own miniature parasol, complete with delicate 'spokes' radiating from the center.
description: The Umbrella Jelly is a small, transparent marine jellyfish with a distinctive dome-shaped bell that resembles a clear umbrella. These delicate creatures typically measure about 1-2 inches across their bell, making them relatively small compared to other jellyfish you might encounter. Their bell is crystal clear with a subtle bluish tint, and you can often see four radial canals running from the center to the edge like the ribs of an umbrella. They pulse gently through the water using rhythmic contractions of their bell.

idTips.label: Bell shape
idTips.description: The bell is distinctly dome-shaped like a perfect umbrella, feeling firm yet gelatinous if gently touched (though handling isn't recommended)

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 1-2 inches across the bell - small enough to fit comfortably in your palm

idTips.label: Transparency
idTips.description: Nearly crystal clear with a faint bluish tinge, so transparent you can easily see through to objects behind it

idTips.label: Radial canals
idTips.description: Four distinct lines running from center to edge of the bell, visible as slightly thicker white or pale lines

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Gentle, rhythmic pulsing motion as it contracts and relaxes its bell to propel through water

habitat: In New England waters, Umbrella Jellies are found in coastal marine environments, particularly in harbors, bays, and nearshore waters. They prefer relatively calm waters and are often spotted near the surface on warm summer days, sometimes drifting close to docks, piers, and rocky shorelines.

seasonality.spring: May begin appearing in warmer coastal waters as temperatures rise, though still uncommon this early in the year.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for sightings, especially in July and August when water temperatures are warmest. Look for them near the surface on calm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline as water temperatures drop, though some may persist into early fall during warm years.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters during the cold winter months.

funFact: **[Uncertain claim flagged]** Umbrella Jellies can actually turn themselves inside-out when stressed or threatened, essentially flipping their umbrella bell backward - imagine turning your umbrella inside-out in a windstorm, except they do it on purpose as a defense mechanism!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small, clear jellyfish like Moon Jellies, but Umbrella Jellies are much smaller and have that distinctive perfect dome shape rather than the flatter, more saucer-like appearance of Moon Jellies. Remember: if it looks like a tiny glass umbrella, you've found the right one!
contextualKnowledge: **[Uncertain claim flagged]** Despite being called a 'jelly,' these creatures are about 95% water and have no brain, blood, or heart - they're essentially living water balloons with a simple nervous system that helps them pulse through the ocean.
compareHints: Since there are no other Eutonina species commonly found in New England waters, compare the Umbrella Jelly to other small hydromedusae in the same family. **[Uncertain claim flagged]** Unlike many of its relatives, the Umbrella Jelly has a particularly pronounced dome shape and fewer, more distinct radial canals. Other small jellies in the area tend to be either flatter or have more complex canal systems.
